Steady since the election

Each dot is one poll and each line a model of its polls, shaded with its 95% interval, so a month with few polls is filled in rather than jumping to whoever reported. Undecided voters are counted out of all voters and soft voters out of those who named a party, so the two charts have different scales.

After preferences v asked once: higher by 6.0 points, a significant gap (95% interval +3.9 to +8.4). It counts the voters who can name a party but won’t rank Labor against the Coalition. Spectre asks both questions of the same voters.

Asked once v after a follow-up: higher by 0.8 points, not a significant gap (95% interval −0.2 to +2.0). A follow-up can only shrink a pollster’s own undecided count, but different pollsters ask each way, so this gap also carries their other differences.

The two pollsters ask different questions with different answers to choose from, so compare each line with itself, not with the other.

National mood‘Is the country heading in the right direction, or on the wrong track?’, Roy Morgan, Essential, SEC Newgate, RedBridge/Accent, Spectre Strategy, Ipsos and McKinnon

More than three in five say Australia is on the wrong track, the most this term

Only 23% say we’re heading in the right direction. Net mood has not changed significantly in a month, though it is down more than 30 points since May 2025.

23.0%Right direction62.4%Wrong track

14.6% unsure

Net −39.5 points, ▼ 1.8 on a month ago, within the margin: a 27% chance it rose

Roy Morgan’s latest release (November) prints Western Australia as the state most convinced the country is on the wrong track (70%), Tasmania the least (61%). Its full state table is paywalled.

How to read this chart

Each dot is one published reading, where its pollster printed it. The lines are a model’s estimate of what the average pollster asking this question would find, day by day, read off month by month; the shading is its 95% interval. There is a 95% chance the figure lies inside it, given the polls and the model’s assumptions.

The model treats the country’s mood as something that moves a little each day, faster or slower as the polls themselves show, and each pollster as seeing it through a lean of its own plus sampling error. It works out the mood and every lean together from all the polls at once, so a pollster that asks often doesn’t outvote the rest, an older poll counts for less the more opinion has moved since, and months with few polls simply carry wider shading.

Pollsters are compared on the ratio of right direction to wrong track, which doesn’t depend on whether “unsure” was offered: Ipsos and SEC Newgate force a choice, so their right and wrong both run higher, and Lowy and McKinnon ask about satisfaction instead. Each is read through its own lean, measured against the others, which can drift slowly. The level is set by the pollsters asking this question, each counting once; the unsure share by those that print one. The notes below say how each asks.

The change on a month ago compares today with the model’s estimate of a month ago using every poll since, and is called significant only when its 95% interval excludes zero. No pollster’s lean can be measured against the truth, only against the others, so an error every pollster shares stays invisible.

The bar over the chart sets the window, as on the confidence charts. It opens on this term; ‹ and › step a term at a time, Term, 10 yrs, 25 yrs and All widen it, and the strip underneath is the whole line in miniature, as its net (right direction less wrong track), with the governments in power beneath it — drag the window, drag its edges to resize, or tap a spot to jump. Longer windows mark each federal election with a faint rule. Dots show only in a term-length window.

Roy Morgan has asked since 2007, Ipsos since September 2016, and the others since 2022 or later, so before September 2016 the line rests on Roy Morgan alone. Its readings can be placed against the others only from later years, and Roy Morgan changed how it polls in 2020 and again in 2022, so the shading there includes how far its lean could have been: the level is uncertain by several points, the month-to-month movement less so.

The dashed lines are Ipsos’ Global Average on the same terms: each wave’s ratio of right to wrong moved by Ipsos’s lean in Australia that month, then split with Australia’s unsure share. That keeps exactly the gap Ipsos itself measures between Australia and the world, and assumes, as any such comparison must, that its Australian and world samples lean alike.

How each pollster asks

“Generally speaking, do you feel that things in Australia are heading in the right direction or would you say things are seriously heading in the wrong direction?”

AnswersRight direction and wrong direction, with a third column printed as “Can’t say / no answer”.

MethodFace-to-face to March 2020, then multi-mode to May 2022; its table records no method since August 2022. Each of the three runs has its own lean, the earlier two placed on today’s scale through the pollsters that polled across each change.

In the lineSets the line’s level with the other pollsters asking this question, each counting once, and feeds its unsure share.

“In general, would you say that Australia is heading in the right direction or on the wrong track?”

AnswersRight direction, wrong track and unsure, each printed. The February–May 2022 reports asked “or is it off on the wrong track?”.

In the lineSets the line’s level with the other pollsters asking this question, each counting once, and feeds its unsure share.

“Overall, do you think Australia, (state/territory), and your local area are heading in the right direction or the wrong direction? (The Australia item is used.)”

AnswersRight direction and wrong direction only, summing to 100. Its reports print a “Don’t know” column for other questions but none for this one, so it is treated as a forced choice.

In the lineSets the line’s level with the other pollsters asking this question, each counting once; its ratio of right to wrong only, as it prints no unsure share.

“Would you say that things in Australia are… generally headed in the right direction; generally headed in the wrong direction; not sure.”

AnswersRight direction, wrong direction and not sure, offered as answers (single select; the first two in random order).

In the lineSets the line’s level with the other pollsters asking this question, each counting once, and feeds its unsure share.

“In your view, is Australia heading in the right direction, or the wrong direction at this time?”

AnswersRight direction, wrong direction and unsure, each printed. The 2025 wording is unverified.

In the lineSets the line’s level with the other pollsters asking this question, each counting once, and feeds its unsure share.

“Generally speaking, do you think that Australia is currently heading in the right direction, or the wrong direction?”

AnswersRight direction and wrong direction; the rest (about 13%) is read as unsure. The third answer’s label is not on file, and the 2023–24 wording is unverified.

In the lineSets the line’s level with the other pollsters asking this question, each counting once, and feeds its unsure share.

“Generally speaking, would you say things in this country are heading in the right direction, or are they off on the wrong track?”

AnswersRight direction and wrong track, summing to 100: Ipsos notes that its totals can leave out “don’t know” or not-stated answers, so no undecided share is printed.

MethodIpsos Online Panel, about 1,000 Australians aged 16–74 a month (16–64 from March to July 2019).

In the lineSets the line’s level with the other pollsters asking this question, each counting once; its ratio of right to wrong only, as it prints no unsure share.

“All things considered, how satisfied are you with the way Australia is heading?”

AnswersSatisfied and dissatisfied (each aggregating two strengths), a neutral middle answer (“neither satisfied nor dissatisfied”, about 15%) and a separate “don’t know” (about 1%).

MethodOnline, about 4,300–4,400 Australians aged 18 and over a year.

In the lineAsks about satisfaction, so it is read through a lean of its own, wide enough that a couple of readings teach the model about the question, not about Australia. It never sets the level or the unsure share.

Note: The dots sit where each pollster printed them: Ipsos and SEC Newgate force a choice and Lowy and McKinnon ask about satisfaction, so theirs sit apart from the line, which is set for the average pollster asking this question.

Economic sentimentConfidence indices, 100 = neutral, five published series

Confidence is underwater on both counts.

Consumers at 66.6, up 3.5 on the week. Consumers on Westpac–MI’s read at 78.2, down 2.2 on the month, not far off its low of 78.2 in Nov 2026. Consumers on DemosAU’s index at 38.7, not far off its low of 38.7 in Nov 2026. Businesses at 81.7, up 5.2 on the month. Businesses on NAB’s survey at −15, down 1 on the month (conditions −2).

How to read this chart

Five published gauges of economic confidence, split into two views — the consumer lanes and the business pair, switched by the tabs over the chart — and set out as each house prints them: the weekly ANZ–Roy Morgan consumer index and monthly business index, Westpac–MI’s monthly consumer sentiment and DemosAU’s national consumer-sentiment index, and NAB’s Monthly Business Survey. Each dot is one release, as printed; each line is the same readings smoothed with a recency-weighted kernel (half-life 14 days on the weekly index, 60 days on the monthly ones), so release-to-release noise reads as trend — the quoted figures stay the raw prints. There is no combining across houses and no adjustment for lean — a record, not an estimate.

The bar over the chart sets the window, and the window holds as you switch tabs. It opens on this term; ‹ and › step back and forward a term at a time, and Term, 10 yrs, 25 yrs and All widen it (‹ › then page back and forward by that length). The strip under each chart is the whole record in miniature with the governments beneath it: drag the window along it, drag its edges to resize it, drag across the strip to draw a new one, or tap a spot to jump there. A term reads off its election — Election, 1 yr, 2 yrs — so every term shares one ruler; a longer window counts calendar years and marks each federal election with a faint rule. Dots show in a window of about a term; longer windows draw the lines alone.

Behind a term the band pools the view’s main gauge over the other terms, each smoothed like the lines (60-day half-life) and lined up on its own election month: the middle half in the heavier fill, the middle 80% in the lighter, their average the dashed line, paler where fewer terms ran that long. This term’s band is every past term; a past term’s is every term but itself. Consumer history runs to 1974, business to 2013. “Draw a past term” lifts any single term out of the band as its own smoothed, dotted line in the house’s own colour — and on the consumer view Westpac–MI’s reading of the same term draws beside it, dotted gold where its 1974 series reaches — and “Source data, CSV” in the footer downloads every release and past-term reading. Before each house’s live release file begins, its line runs on through the house’s own monthly history, smoothed the same way and drawn a little thinner — ANZ–Roy Morgan’s consumer index to 1973, Westpac–MI’s consumer sentiment to 1974, Roy Morgan’s business index to 2010, NAB’s printed net balance to March 1997. Westpac–MI months before 2010 come from the OECD’s republication of the index, which rounds them to the nearest whole index point; from 2010 the RBA’s table carries Westpac–MI’s own decimals.

ANZ–Roy Morgan’s and Westpac–MI’s are indices where 100 is neutral; DemosAU’s national index is 50-neutral and draws doubled to share the line. NAB instead reports a net balance — the share of optimistic firms minus pessimistic ones — where 0 is neutral, so the NAB line is drawn 100 points up to share the neutral line on the business view; the figure beside it and in its tooltips is NAB’s own printed number, and the row also carries the survey’s conditions reading.

The Inflation & growth tab sets the ABS’s and OECD’s official figures out as seven small charts that share the window, Australia in colour and the OECD in grey. Inflation: Australia’s headline inflation (the ABS’s monthly all-items CPI as an annual change; before the monthly CPI era, the quarterly series derived from the ABS’s own published index numbers, spliced where the printed monthly measure begins) beside the OECD-wide average and the median member country, with the Reserve Bank’s 2–3% target shaded from August 1996, when it was adopted. Inflation against target: Australia’s figure minus the band’s 2.5% midpoint, beside the median member’s distance from its own central bank’s target (band targets read at their midpoints; a country joins the median only once both its print and a formal target exist that month, so the line grows as inflation targeting spread after New Zealand’s 1990 band). Growth per person: real GDP per person, real net national disposable income per person and real household disposable income per person (annual change in chain-volume levels, seasonally adjusted), beside real GDP per person across the OECD (the OECD’s household dashboard index, so the grey line begins in 2008) and the median member’s own GDP-per-person growth computed here from the OECD’s growth and population files. National income is the whole country’s: it counts what exports buy and income paid abroad, and includes companies’ and governments’ income. Household income is what households have after tax and interest — the ABS’s household gross disposable income over its household consumption price deflator and its population, worked out here because the ABS prints no real per-person figure (it matches the OECD’s own calculation for Australia to within 0.2 points). Its Actual switch shows the three Australian series as dollars instead (each seasonally adjusted quarter at its annual rate, in 2023–24 prices). Productivity: GDP per hour worked — the ABS’s seasonally adjusted index as an annual rate, beside the OECD members’ median output-per-worker growth (computed here from their own file, which carries no per-hour median, so the two lines measure differently and the page names a basis openly). Its Increase/Actual switch swaps the yearly rate for the index itself — the form in which the decade since roughly 2016, nearly flat beside the two before it, reads as a level rather than a wiggle. Earnings: the real change in full-time adult ordinary-time weekly earnings — the ABS’s nominal print deflated here by its own consumer price index, since the ABS publishes no real figure — beside the median of the OECD countries’ real average-wage year changes, a different measure and cadence (annual gross wages per employee at constant 2023 purchasing-power prices). Unemployment: the ABS’s monthly seasonally adjusted rate, a level rather than an annual change, beside the OECD members’ median harmonised rate, computed here. Income inequality: the Gini coefficient of household income after tax, adjusted for household size (0 would be everyone on the same income, 1 one household holding it all), from two surveys kept as separate lines because their levels differ — the HILDA survey every year from 2002–03, and the ABS’s own Survey of Income and Housing, the official measure, about every second year from 1994–95 to 2019–20 (the ABS has scheduled no next release) — beside the OECD member countries’ median coefficient, computed here; the OECD publishes no OECD-wide Gini. Both surveys run years behind the other charts, so a recent window can hold no survey year at all; the chart then names the latest. Nothing is smoothed, adjusted, combined or estimated — official prints, joined as-is, refreshed daily from the ABS and OECD data APIs (the deviation lines, the OECD medians and Australia’s real-earnings deflation are computed here: Australia’s from the ABS’s own figures, the OECD medians from the member countries’ OECD-published prints and, since 2026, from the OECD’s monthly inflation release table — one decimal, three on the Gini lines).

Reading economic sentiment beside the polls is context, not a predictor of the vote. The consumer and business gauges needn’t move together, and two houses asking differently worded questions needn’t agree week to week.

Release calendar

The next editions of the four gauges charted above — ANZ–Roy Morgan’s and Westpac–MI’s consumer series, Roy Morgan’s and NAB’s business series — projected from each series’ own release rhythm, exactly as the Latest-polls calendar projects a pollster. A date is the earliest a release could land, never a promise; a series that misses its slot stays listed in the due lead-in until the release is recorded.

Note: The consumer and business confidence indices are displayed here just for extra context in today’s low-confidence environment.

About this page

The modern page in old clothes

Every headline, figure and chart here is the modern front page’s own, read from it each time the site is built and drawn the way a website of about 2000 would have drawn it. Where a modern section switches between views, its panel here offers the same switch.

More in the modern view

The modern page adds tooltips and time ranges to its charts, the primary vote by pollster or group of voters, and each latest poll opened in full. All polls and Past cycles have retro views too, and so does the Electoral map.

auspol tracker is an unofficial aggregator of published federal opinion polling.

Best efforts are made to make the aggregate figures transparent, trustworthy, statistically sound, and informative, but they are, in the end, estimates only.

How the figures are built is in Info. Spot an error, a missing poll, or have any other feedback? Please let me know.
